questions.subtopic: Intrusion Detection Methods. Anomaly Baseline Integrity
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-94 (Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SI-4(13) (Analyze Traffic and Event Patterns)
questions.question: An anomaly-based intrusion detection system learned its baseline during a month when, it was later found, an attacker was copying data out. Which risk should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Security analysts may need fresh training on the sensor's console
options.B: The sensor may raise many false alarms on legitimate traffic
options.C: The attacker's file transfers may be treated as normal activity
options.D: Signature updates for the sensor may have lapsed that month

questions.key_concept: An anomaly baseline learned while an attacker is active absorbs the attack as normal, producing false negatives.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the sensor counted as normal while it was learning.
questions.correct_explanation: An anomaly-based sensor treats whatever it saw while learning as normal. If an attacker was active during that period, the exfiltration became part of the baseline and will raise no alert, a false negative. The baseline must be relearned from a known-clean period. A flood of false alarms is the closest choice: it is the usual weakness of anomaly detection, but a poisoned baseline makes the sensor miss the attacker instead.

wrong_explanations.A: Training may help analysts, but the sensor's flaw lies in what it learned, not in how staff use its console.
wrong_explanations.B: Extra false alarms are the usual drawback of anomaly detection, but a poisoned baseline causes the opposite problem: missed attacks.
wrong_explanations.D: Anomaly-based detection works from a learned baseline rather than signatures, so update timing does not explain this outcome.

tips: Eliminate: A blames the analysts' training, and D blames signatures, which an anomaly baseline does not rely on.
Final two: C beats B because a baseline learned during an attack makes that attack look normal, so it goes unflagged.
Exam cue: learn anomaly baselines in clean periods and relearn them when the business changes, or the attack becomes normal.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-26 (Decoys); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-7 (Boundary Protection)
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a newly deployed honeypot that imitates a payroll database server. Which finding represents the GREATEST risk?

options.A: The honeypot can connect directly to production servers
options.B: The honeypot has recorded no interactions since it went live
options.C: Honeypot alerts go to a shared mailbox reviewed once a week
options.D: The honeypot runs an older database version than production

questions.key_concept: Honeypots must be isolated from production and monitored; a decoy that connects to real systems becomes an attacker's foothold.
questions.pre_read: Ask which finding turns the decoy from a detection tool into a route for attackers.
questions.correct_explanation: A decoy that can reach production gives any attacker who compromises it a launch point into real systems, so the deception tool now adds risk instead of reducing it. Decoys must be isolated. Weekly review of alerts nearly wins: it wastes the honeypot's high-confidence alerts and delays response, but it weakens detection rather than opening a new path to production.

wrong_explanations.B: Silence is normal for a decoy nobody should use; it may prompt a check of placement, but it is not a risk in itself.
wrong_explanations.C: Slow review wastes the honeypot's strong alerts, but it limits detection; it does not open a route into production systems.
wrong_explanations.D: A decoy is meant to look attractive, and an older version can make it more convincing to an intruder.

tips: Eliminate: B describes the normal state of a decoy, and D a version gap that can make it more convincing.
Final two: A beats C because a poorly isolated decoy becomes a foothold; slow monitoring weakens detection but opens no path.
Exam cue: deception adds detection, not prevention. A decoy must be isolated and watched, or it adds risk.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-26 (Decoys); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SI-4 (System Monitoring)
questions.question: Concerned about staff browsing payroll data, management plants a fake executive salary file that no business process uses. What should the IS auditor identify as the PRIMARY benefit of this control?

options.A: It stops insiders from opening the real salary records
options.B: It removes the need for periodic access reviews on the share
options.C: It draws curious staff away from the genuine payroll files
options.D: Any access to the file gives a high-confidence alert

questions.key_concept: A honeytoken has no legitimate use, so any access to it is a high-confidence, low-noise detective alert.
questions.pre_read: Decide whether the control prevents, detects or corrects before weighing its benefit.
questions.correct_explanation: Because no legitimate process uses the fake file, anyone who opens it is almost certainly misusing access, so each alert is high-confidence with very few false alarms. That is the honeytoken's main benefit: detection. Diverting staff from real files is the strongest alternative, a common belief about decoys, but a curious insider can still open the genuine records; the decoy reveals misuse rather than preventing it.

wrong_explanations.A: The decoy file changes no permissions, so anyone who can reach the real salary records can still open them.
wrong_explanations.B: Spotting misuse after the fact does not replace periodic reviews that remove unneeded access before it can be misused.
wrong_explanations.C: Some decoys can deflect attackers, but one fake file beside the real records does not keep insiders away from them; management's stated aim is to catch browsing, which is detection.

tips: Eliminate: A expects the decoy to block access, and B lets it replace access reviews; it does neither.
Final two: D beats C because a decoy detects misuse with little noise; it does not keep anyone from the real records.
Exam cue: honeypots and honeytokens are detective controls. Their value is high-confidence alerts, not prevention.

questions.subtopic: Cloud Deployment Models. Choosing a Model
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.23 (Information Security for Use of Cloud Services)
questions.question: A university wants to move export-controlled research data to the cheapest cloud platform it can find. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Choose the lowest-cost public cloud provider with an in-country region
options.B: Move to a private cloud, which isolates data from other tenants
options.C: Have the data owner set the data's legal and handling requirements
options.D: Review shortlisted providers' assurance reports for scope and exceptions

questions.key_concept: Choose a cloud deployment model from data sensitivity, legal duties and risk appetite, with the data owner accountable, not from cost alone.
questions.pre_read: When cost drives a cloud move, ask who has assessed the data's legal and sensitivity requirements.
questions.correct_explanation: The deployment model must follow data sensitivity, legal duties and risk appetite, not cost alone. A documented risk assessment of legal duties, such as export control and residency, and classification, approved by the data owner who stays accountable, sets the requirements every option must meet. Reviewing providers' assurance reports is the most tempting alternative: it is needed, but only once the requirements exist, because without them management cannot judge whether a report's scope is adequate.

wrong_explanations.A: Picking on price with an in-country region treats location as the only duty and skips the sensitivity and risk decision the data owner must make.
wrong_explanations.B: A private cloud removes co-tenant risk, but choosing a model before assessing the data's requirements is premature; export rules may still restrict who administers it.
wrong_explanations.D: Assurance reports matter, but without agreed requirements management cannot tell whether a report's scope covers what this data needs.

tips: Eliminate: A lets price drive the choice, and B picks a model before the requirements are known.
Final two: C beats D because requirements come first; provider reports can only be judged against them.
Exam cue: the cloud model follows data sensitivity, legal duties and risk appetite, not cost; the data owner stays accountable.

questions.subtopic: Cloud Deployment Models. Community Cloud Governance
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.23 (Information Security for Use of Cloud Services)
questions.question: Four regional water utilities with identical regulatory obligations have moved to a shared community cloud. What should the IS auditor verify FIRST?

options.A: The cloud provider's latest SOC 2 Type 2 assurance report
options.B: An agreement assigning each utility's control and oversight duties
options.C: Each utility's own continuity plan for the shared platform
options.D: Each utility's quarterly review of its own users' access

questions.key_concept: In a community cloud, several organizations share one platform, so an agreement must first set who controls and oversees what.
questions.pre_read: Notice that several organizations share one platform. Ask what must be settled before anyone can rely on its controls.
questions.correct_explanation: When several utilities share one community cloud, no single organization controls it by default, so the auditor first verifies an agreement that assigns each party's control and oversight duties, including who manages the provider. The provider's SOC 2 report is the tempting option: it is valuable evidence, but it covers only the provider's controls, and without agreed duties no one may be responsible for acting on it.

wrong_explanations.A: A SOC 2 Type 2 report (an independent opinion on a provider's controls over time) is useful, but it cannot say which utility owns which shared control.
wrong_explanations.C: A utility's own continuity plan matters, but it cannot cover shared recovery duties that no agreement has yet assigned.
wrong_explanations.D: Each utility can review its own users, but administrator access to the shared platform falls to no one until duties are agreed.

tips: Eliminate: C and D are controls each utility runs alone; until duties are agreed, shared parts of the platform fall to no one.
Final two: B beats A because agreed duties must exist before the provider's report can be acted on; the report covers only the provider.
Exam cue: when several parties share one platform, first confirm a written split of control and oversight duties.

questions.framework_ref: CSA Cloud Controls Matrix v4 (IAM, LOG and CCC domains); ISO/IEC 27017 (Cloud Security)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a bank's private cloud and its public cloud each use separate administrator accounts, logging and configuration baselines. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Have each cloud team formally document its own baseline
options.B: Assign separate audit teams to review each environment every year
options.C: Deploy additional monitoring tools in the public cloud environment
options.D: Apply one common control standard and identity source to both

questions.key_concept: Hybrid and multi-cloud designs need one common control standard and identity source across every environment, or gaps open at the seams.
questions.pre_read: In a hybrid design, ask what happens to accounts and evidence when activity crosses between environments.
questions.correct_explanation: In a hybrid design, gaps sit at the seams: an administrator removed in one environment may keep access in the other, and an attack crossing between them leaves evidence in logs nobody correlates. One common control standard and identity source across both closes those seams. More monitoring in the public cloud comes closest: it strengthens one side but leaves identities and baselines inconsistent between environments.

wrong_explanations.A: Documenting each baseline records the split instead of closing it; separate accounts and uncorrelated logs stay in place.
wrong_explanations.B: More audit teams would report the inconsistency each year but would not fix the separate accounts, logs and baselines causing it.
wrong_explanations.C: Extra tools in one environment improve its visibility, but accounts and baselines stay inconsistent and cross-environment activity stays uncorrelated.

tips: Eliminate: A documents the split instead of closing it, and B adds audits without fixing the cause.
Final two: D beats C because hybrid risk sits between environments; strengthening one side leaves the seams open.
Exam cue: in hybrid and multi-cloud designs, look for one common control standard and identity source across every environment.

questions.framework_ref: ONF TR-511 (Principles and Practices for Securing Software-Defined Networks); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IA-9 (Service Identification and Authentication)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that any internal server can call the application programming interface (API) of a firm's software-defined network controller without authenticating. What is the GREATEST risk?

options.A: Switches could run out of memory for forwarding rules
options.B: Interface calls could slow the forwarding of user packets
options.C: One compromised host could redirect or drop any traffic
options.D: Unauthenticated callers could map the full routing layout

questions.key_concept: An SDN controller's programming interfaces can change the whole network, so they need authentication, authorization and logging.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the interface lets a caller do, not just what it lets a caller see.
questions.correct_explanation: The controller decides where all traffic goes, and its programming interface accepts change requests. Without authentication, any compromised internal server could push rules that reroute, intercept or drop traffic anywhere in the network. Exposure of the routing layout is the closest choice: reconnaissance matters, but an interface that accepts changes lets an attacker alter the network itself, a far greater integrity and availability risk.

wrong_explanations.A: An unauthenticated caller could fill flow tables, but that is one narrow effect; the same access lets an attacker reroute or drop any traffic.
wrong_explanations.B: Interface calls are control-plane traffic to the controller; switches keep forwarding user packets in the data plane.
wrong_explanations.D: Seeing the routing layout helps an attacker plan, but an interface that accepts changes lets that attacker reroute or drop traffic directly.

tips: Eliminate: A is one narrow effect of the same access, and B mixes up the control plane with the data plane that forwards packets.
Final two: C beats D because the interface accepts changes; altering the network outweighs merely learning its layout.
Exam cue: whoever can instruct the SDN controller controls the network; its interfaces need authentication, authorization and logging.

questions.framework_ref: ONF TR-511 (Principles and Practices for Securing Software-Defined Networks); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.22 (Segregation of Networks); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-7 (Boundary Protection)
questions.question: A hospital's software-defined network controller requires administrator sign-in, but its management interface is reachable from every staff device. Which recommendation is MOST important for the IS auditor to make?

options.A: Restrict controller access to a separate administration network
options.B: Alert the security team to every controller configuration change
options.C: Add a standby controller in another server room
options.D: Keep daily controller configuration backups on separate storage

questions.key_concept: Sign-in alone is not enough for an SDN controller; its management interface should be reachable only from a restricted administration network.
questions.pre_read: Notice that sign-in is required yet every staff device can reach the controller. Ask what limits the exposure if a password or device is compromised.
questions.correct_explanation: Whoever controls the SDN controller can reroute or block traffic across the hospital, and sign-in alone fails once a password is phished or a staff device is compromised. Restricting the management interface to a separate administration network removes that exposure as a second layer. Alerting on configuration changes nearly wins: it helps spot misuse, but only after an attacker has already changed how the network behaves.

wrong_explanations.B: Change alerts, like a separate admin network, guard the controller, yet they fire after rerouting; limit who can reach control points.
wrong_explanations.C: A standby improves availability, but it leaves the management interface open to every staff device.
wrong_explanations.D: Backups speed recovery after damage, but they do not stop anyone on the staff network reaching the controller.

tips: Eliminate: C improves availability and D speeds recovery; neither limits who can reach the controller.
Final two: A beats B because restricting access prevents misuse of the controller, while change alerts only detect it afterward.
Exam cue: centralized control planes need layered protection; isolate their management access, even behind sign-in, before adding detection.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-5 (Denial-of-Service Protection); NIST SP 800-189 (Resilient Interdomain Traffic Exchange: BGP Security and DDoS Mitigation)
questions.question: A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) flood filled an online broker's internet links for six hours, halting trading. Which control should the IS auditor recommend as BEST to prevent a repeat?

options.A: Firewalls with higher throughput and stricter rate limits
options.B: Blocking the source addresses logged during the attack
options.C: Endpoint detection and response tools on the trading servers
options.D: Upstream scrubbing arranged in advance with a provider

questions.key_concept: Volumetric denial-of-service floods fill the internet link first, so mitigation must sit upstream and be contracted in advance.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the attack overwhelms the service, then pick a defense that sits in front of that point.
questions.correct_explanation: A flood large enough to fill the internet links overwhelms them before any traffic reaches on-site equipment, so the defense must sit upstream. Scrubbing arranged in advance with a provider diverts and filters attack traffic and passes clean traffic on. Stronger firewalls come closest: they help against smaller or application-level attacks, but they sit behind the saturated link and never see most of the flood.

wrong_explanations.A: Faster firewalls with rate limits would handle floods the link can carry. This one filled the link itself; volumetric attacks must be filtered upstream.
wrong_explanations.B: Distributed attacks come from thousands of hijacked devices whose addresses change, so blocking past sources does not stop the next flood.
wrong_explanations.C: Endpoint tools detect malicious code on servers; they cannot stop traffic that fills the links before reaching the servers.

tips: Eliminate: B blocks yesterday's sources in a botnet that keeps changing, and C targets malware, not traffic floods.
Final two: D beats A because a flood that fills the link arrives before the firewall; only filtering upstream can absorb it.
Exam cue: match the defense to where the attack works; volumetric floods need upstream mitigation arranged before the attack.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-7 (Boundary Protection); NIST SP 800-83 Rev 1 (Malware Incident Prevention and Handling)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a firm's database servers may open connections to any internet address and port. What is the PRIMARY risk of this setting?

options.A: Attackers on the internet could reach the servers directly
options.B: Malware could send stolen records to attacker-controlled systems
options.C: Administrators could install unapproved software from vendor sites
options.D: The servers could use more bandwidth than the link allows

questions.key_concept: Egress filtering limits outbound traffic to approved destinations, cutting malware's command channel and a key exfiltration path.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an infected server needs to do over the network once it is compromised.
questions.correct_explanation: Outbound rules decide where internal systems may send traffic. With none, malware on a database server can reach its command and control (C2) server and move stolen records out over any port. Egress filtering to approved destinations cuts both channels. Unapproved software downloads are the most tempting alternative: open outbound access makes them easier, but change control and administrator rights govern installs, so the open path for theft is the greater exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: Inbound connections are governed by separate inbound rules; open outbound access does not by itself let outsiders reach the servers.
wrong_explanations.C: Open outbound access makes downloads easier, but installs are governed mainly by change control and administrator rights, not egress rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Bandwidth use is a capacity concern; it is not the security exposure that open outbound access creates.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses outbound rules with inbound access, and D is a capacity concern, not a security exposure.
Final two: B beats C because an open outbound path lets malware take orders and carry data out; installs fall under change control.
Exam cue: egress filtering limits which destinations malware can reach for commands and narrows the paths stolen data can leave by.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-167 (Guide to Application Whitelisting); NIST SP 800-83 Rev 1 (Malware Incident Prevention and Handling)
questions.question: Custom malware that antivirus signatures did not recognize ran on a retailer's point-of-sale terminals, which use a fixed set of programs. Which control should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Application allowlisting that blocks any unapproved executable
options.B: Antivirus signature updates pushed several times a day
options.C: Behavior-based detection that alerts analysts to suspicious activity
options.D: Security awareness training for store cashiers and managers

questions.key_concept: Application allowlisting blocks any unapproved program, stopping new malware that signatures miss; it suits fixed-function devices best.
questions.pre_read: Notice the devices run a fixed set of programs, then ask which control can block anything outside that set.
questions.correct_explanation: Point-of-sale terminals run a small, fixed set of programs, so application allowlisting is practical: anything not on the approved list cannot run, including custom code no signature has seen. Behavior-based detection comes closest: it can spot new malware, but it alerts after the code is already running and needs analysts to act, while allowlisting stops it from running at all.

wrong_explanations.B: Signatures match only code already seen; more frequent updates still miss custom malware written for this attack.
wrong_explanations.C: Behavior detection can catch new code, but it acts after the code runs; on fixed-function devices, prevention by allowlisting is stronger.
wrong_explanations.D: Training helps against tricks aimed at people, but it puts no technical barrier on the terminals against code that should never run.

tips: Eliminate: B still depends on signatures that custom code lacks, and D relies on people instead of a technical control on the device.
Final two: A beats C because allowlisting stops unapproved code before it runs; behavior detection only raises an alert afterward.
Exam cue: where devices run a fixed set of programs, allowlisting is the strongest malware control; signatures miss new code.
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Malware. Application Allowlisting on Fixed-Function Devices'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 5B2.1 (Wave 1 coverage batch Q2: a subtopic with no practice yet). Public sources: NIST.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-83 Rev 1 (Malware Incident Prevention and Handling); MITRE ATT&CK T1014 (Rootkit)
questions.question: Scanning a breached server's disk from a trusted computer found malware the server's own tools never showed. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST before it returns to service?

options.A: Run a full scan with updated tools on the server itself
options.B: Remove each malware file the outside scan identified
options.C: Reset administrator passwords and then return it to service
options.D: Rebuild it from known-good media and restore verified data

questions.key_concept: Once malware has hidden from a system's own tools, the system cannot be trusted; rebuild it from known-good media and verified data.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether any cleanup done on this server could prove that nothing hidden remains.
questions.correct_explanation: Malware that hid from the server's own tools points to a rootkit, so the operating system itself can no longer be trusted to report what remains. Rebuilding from known-good media and restoring verified data returns the server to a state that can be trusted. Removing each file the outside scan found is the closest choice: it cleans what was seen, but cannot prove nothing else stays hidden or altered.

wrong_explanations.A: The server's own tools already missed the malware once; a scan run inside a compromised system cannot be trusted to report the truth.
wrong_explanations.B: Deleting the known files removes only what the outside scan saw; hidden components or altered system files may remain.
wrong_explanations.C: New passwords help after credential theft, but the hidden malware stays on the server and can capture the new passwords.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts tools that already failed to see the malware, and C changes passwords but leaves the malware in place.
Final two: D beats B because removal cleans only what was seen; a rebuild restores a state that can be trusted.
Exam cue: when malware hides from a system's own tools, suspect a rootkit; rebuild from known-good media rather than cleaning in place.
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Malware Types. Rootkits and Rebuilding From Trusted Media'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 5B2.1 (Wave 1 coverage batch Q2: a subtopic with no practice yet). Public sources: NIST, MITRE.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-131A Rev 2 (Transitioning the Use of Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Lengths); NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 (Recommendation for Key Management)
questions.question: A laboratory application still encrypts result files with Triple DES, which current standards no longer allow for encryption, and the vendor notes no breach has occurred. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the vendor's view, since no breach has been reported
options.B: Use the longest keying option Triple DES supports
options.C: Migrate to AES by a date the data owner sets
options.D: Add monitoring of who opens the encrypted result files

questions.key_concept: A retired cipher should be replaced on a dated plan owned by the data owner; monitoring only compensates, and reusing the old cipher fixes nothing.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each action fixes the weak cipher itself or only works around it.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST no longer allows Triple DES for encryption, so the files lack the assurance a current cipher gives, whatever the incident history. Migrating to the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) by a date the data owner approves fixes the root cause and assigns accountability for it. Monitoring who opens the files nearly wins: it may detect misuse, but copies taken from the system stay under a retired cipher.

wrong_explanations.A: No reported breach is not evidence of strength; NIST retired the cipher because its assurance no longer meets current standards.
wrong_explanations.B: Keying options do not rescue Triple DES; the cipher itself is retired for encryption, whichever key option is used.
wrong_explanations.D: Access monitoring is a valid compensating control pending a fix. But the retired cipher stays: compensation bridges to remediation, never replaces it.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the absence of a reported breach as proof of strength, and B changes key options on a cipher that is retired regardless.
Final two: C beats D because replacing the cipher fixes the root cause; monitoring only compensates for it.
Exam cue: when an algorithm is retired, recommend a dated migration that the business owns, not a compensating control around it.

questions.subtopic: Symmetric Encryption. One Key Shared Across Many Devices
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 (Recommendation for Key Management); NISTIR 8259A (IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline)
questions.question: A utility ships every smart meter with the same AES key built into its firmware to protect the readings sent to head office. Which risk should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: Changing the key later needs a firmware update on every meter
options.B: Meters may lack the processing power that AES requires
options.C: Readings could arrive late when the network is congested
options.D: One extracted key exposes every meter's readings

questions.key_concept: A symmetric key shared by every device is only as safe as the least protected device; each device needs its own key.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an attacker gains by extracting the key from a single meter.
questions.correct_explanation: Because every meter holds the same Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) key, that key is only as safe as the least protected meter: anyone who pulls it from one device's firmware can read, and forge, readings from the whole fleet. The cost of changing a built-in key is the strongest alternative; it is real, but it slows the response after a compromise rather than being the exposure itself. Unique keys per device limit the damage.

wrong_explanations.A: A costly key change is a real drawback, but it follows from the shared key; the exposure of every meter is the larger risk.
wrong_explanations.B: AES is designed to run efficiently on small devices, so processing power is not the main concern here.
wrong_explanations.C: Network delay affects timeliness, not the confidentiality of readings protected by a shared key.

tips: Eliminate: B doubts that AES can run on small devices, which it is designed to do, and C is a network timing issue.
Final two: D beats A because one extracted key exposes the whole fleet; a costly key change only slows the response.
Exam cue: when one symmetric key is shared by many devices or parties, the greatest risk is that a single leak exposes them all.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 (Recommendation for Key Management); NIST SP 800-175B Rev 1 (Guideline for Using Cryptographic Standards in the Federal Government: Cryptographic Mechanisms)
questions.question: A partner emails a payroll file encrypted with AES-256 and includes the decryption key in the same message. What is the PRIMARY weakness the IS auditor should report?

options.A: Anyone holding the email can read the payroll file
options.B: The partner may reuse the same key for later files
options.C: AES-256 is too weak a cipher for payroll data
options.D: Email size limits may corrupt a large encrypted file

questions.key_concept: Encryption protects data only while the key stays apart from it; deliver keys through a separate, protected channel.
questions.pre_read: Ask who could read the payroll file if the email were forwarded or intercepted.
questions.correct_explanation: Sending the key with the data defeats the encryption: anyone who intercepts, forwards or later finds the email holds both the file and the key needed to read it. The key must travel by a separate, protected route. Reuse of the same key for later files is the most tempting alternative: it widens the damage of any leak, but this key is already exposed with the very file it protects.

wrong_explanations.B: Key reuse widens the damage of a leak, but this key is already exposed with the very file it protects.
wrong_explanations.C: AES-256 is a current, strong cipher; the weakness lies in how the key was sent, not in the algorithm.
wrong_explanations.D: Size limits are an operational issue; they do not expose the payroll data to anyone.

tips: Eliminate: C blames a strong cipher, and D is a delivery problem that exposes no data.
Final two: A beats B because a key sent with the file lets any reader decrypt it now; key reuse only widens later exposure.
Exam cue: the algorithm is rarely the weak point; check how the key is delivered and stored, apart from the data.

questions.framework_ref: NIST FIPS 186-5 (Digital Signature Standard (DSS)); NIST SP 800-175B Rev 1 (Guideline for Using Cryptographic Standards in the Federal Government: Cryptographic Mechanisms)
questions.question: An insurer's sales team emails digitally signed price quotes to brokers, believing the signatures stop rival brokers from reading the prices. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Sign each quote with a stronger hashing algorithm
options.B: Also encrypt quotes with each broker's public key
options.C: Sign each quote with the broker's private key
options.D: Limit the quote mailbox to named sales staff

questions.key_concept: A digital signature never hides content; confidentiality needs encryption with the recipient's public key.
questions.pre_read: Ask which security property the sales team actually needs, and whether a signature can provide it.
questions.correct_explanation: A digital signature proves who sent a quote and that it was not changed, but it leaves the content readable to anyone who handles the email. Encrypting each quote with the broker's public key means only that broker's private key can open it. Limiting the sales mailbox comes closest: it narrows access inside the insurer but leaves quotes readable in transit and on the brokers' mail systems.

wrong_explanations.A: A stronger hash improves the signature's integrity check but still leaves every quote readable.
wrong_explanations.C: The insurer never holds a broker's private key, and signing with any key does not hide the content.
wrong_explanations.D: Mailbox limits narrow access inside the insurer but leave quotes readable in transit and on the brokers' mail systems.

tips: Eliminate: A strengthens the signature, which gives integrity, not secrecy, and C uses a private key that the insurer would never hold.
Final two: B beats D because encryption protects each quote wherever it travels; mailbox limits guard only one stop.
Exam cue: signatures give integrity, origin and non-repudiation, never confidentiality; secrecy needs encryption with the recipient's public key.

questions.subtopic: Digital Signatures. MAC vs Signature for Non-Repudiation
questions.framework_ref: NIST FIPS 198-1 (The Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code (HMAC)); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-10 (Non-repudiation)
questions.question: Two trading partners authenticate payment instructions with a message authentication code (MAC) using a shared secret key. If one partner denies sending an instruction, what will the IS auditor MOST LIKELY conclude?

options.A: The code proves which partner created the disputed instruction
options.B: Either key holder could have produced the same code
options.C: The code failed because it does not hide the instruction
options.D: The key's length decides whether the code can be trusted

questions.key_concept: A MAC proves integrity between holders of a shared key but cannot show which holder acted, so it gives no non-repudiation.
questions.pre_read: Ask who else, besides the sender, could have produced a valid code.
questions.correct_explanation: A message authentication code shows an instruction was not changed and came from someone holding the shared key, but both partners hold that key. Either could have produced a valid code, so it cannot show a third party which one sent the instruction. Believing the code identifies the sender is the closest choice; only a digital signature made with one party's private key supports non-repudiation.

wrong_explanations.A: Both partners can compute the same code, so it cannot single out the sender; that needs a private-key signature.
wrong_explanations.C: A MAC is designed for integrity and origin between key holders, not secrecy, so not hiding content is no failure.
wrong_explanations.D: Key length affects resistance to guessing; it cannot show which of two key holders produced the code.

tips: Eliminate: C faults the code for not hiding content, which it never aims to do, and D confuses key strength with proof of sender.
Final two: B beats A because a shared key lets either holder make a valid code; only a private-key signature singles one out.
Exam cue: when a party denies an action, look for a private-key signature; shared-secret codes cannot give non-repudiation.

questions.subtopic: Digital Signatures. Trusting the Verification Key
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-89 (Recommendation for Obtaining Assurances for Digital Signature Applications); NIST FIPS 186-5 (Digital Signature Standard (DSS))
questions.question: An accounts payable system checks each supplier invoice's digital signature using the public key attached to that same invoice file. Which concern should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Invoices signed with revoked supplier keys could still pass checks
options.B: Each invoice exposes the supplier's private signing key
options.C: Fraudsters could sign fake invoices with their own keys
options.D: Checking every signature could slow down invoice processing

questions.key_concept: Verify signatures with a public key from a trusted certificate or registered record, never a key supplied with the signed item.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the system knows the attached public key really belongs to the supplier.
questions.correct_explanation: A signature check proves only that the invoice matches the key used to verify it. If that key arrives inside the invoice, a fraudster can sign a fake invoice with a private key of their own and attach the matching public key, and the check passes. Keys must come from a trusted certificate or the supplier's registered record. Missing revocation checks nearly win: they matter, but a forger never needs a revoked key.

wrong_explanations.A: Missing revocation checks matter, but a key taken from the invoice lets anyone sign; revocation never comes into play.
wrong_explanations.B: Only the public key travels with a signed invoice; the private key stays with the signer.
wrong_explanations.D: Signature checks are fast; any delay is minor beside the fraud that the flawed check allows.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes a private key travels with the invoice, and D raises a minor speed concern.
Final two: C beats A because a key taken from the invoice lets anyone sign; revocation checks never come into play.
Exam cue: a signature is only as trustworthy as the source of the public key used to check it; that key must come from a trusted certificate.

questions.subtopic: PKI Chain of Trust. Governing the Trusted Root Store
questions.framework_ref: IETF RFC 5280 (Internet X.509 PKI Certificate and CRL Profile); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-17 (Public Key Infrastructure Certificates)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that desktop support staff can add root certificates to the trusted store on every company laptop without approval. Which concern is MOST significant?

options.A: A rogue root could make forged sites look genuine
options.B: Laptops could run out of space to store certificates
options.C: Expired roots could stay in the store without anyone noticing
options.D: Staff could see more certificate warnings on internal sites

questions.key_concept: Systems trust any certificate that chains to a root in their store, so changes to trusted roots need approval and logging.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a laptop will trust once someone adds a new root certificate.
questions.correct_explanation: Every laptop trusts any certificate that chains to a root in its store. If unapproved roots can be added, an attacker or careless technician can insert one, issue certificates for any website and intercept staff traffic without a single warning. Changes to trust anchors need approval and logging. Expired roots left in the store are the strongest alternative: untidy, but they let no one create new certificates the laptops trust.

wrong_explanations.B: Root certificates are small files; storage space is not a realistic concern.
wrong_explanations.C: Leftover expired roots are untidy, but they do not let anyone create new certificates the laptops trust.
wrong_explanations.D: Adding roots makes more certificates trusted, so warnings would fall, not rise; the danger is silent trust.

tips: Eliminate: B worries about storage for small files, and D gets the effect backwards, since added roots reduce warnings.
Final two: A beats C because a new root lets anyone issue trusted certificates; an expired root grants nothing new.
Exam cue: the trust anchor sits at the top of every chain, so control who can change the trusted root store.

questions.framework_ref: IETF RFC 5280 (Internet X.509 PKI Certificate and CRL Profile), 4.2.1.3 Key Usage and 4.2.1.9 Basic Constraints; NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-17 (Public Key Infrastructure Certificates)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds a web server's certificate from the internal public key infrastructure (PKI) carries certificate-signing rights like an intermediate certificate authority (CA). What is the PRIMARY risk if that server is breached?

options.A: Attackers could create certificates that company systems trust
options.B: The internal root CA's private key would be exposed
options.C: The server's certificate would expire sooner than planned
options.D: Visitors would see warnings when opening the server's site

questions.key_concept: End-entity certificates must not be able to issue others; if one can, its stolen key can create certificates the organization trusts.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the server's private key can now sign that it never should.
questions.correct_explanation: An end-entity certificate should not be able to issue others. Because this one can, whoever steals the server's private key can sign certificates for any name, and company systems will trust them because the chain leads back to the internal root. Exposure of the root CA's key is the most tempting alternative: it would be worse, but that key is not on the web server, so this breach does not reveal it.

wrong_explanations.B: The root's private key stays with the root CA, ideally offline; breaching the web server does not reveal it.
wrong_explanations.C: A breach does not change a certificate's validity dates; expiry is not the risk here.
wrong_explanations.D: The certificate stays valid and trusted, so visitors see no warnings; the danger is silent misuse.

tips: Eliminate: C and D describe effects a breach would not cause, since the certificate's dates and trust are unchanged.
Final two: A beats B because the stolen server key can now sign trusted certificates; the root's own key is not on that server.
Exam cue: end-entity certificates must not be able to issue others; check the permitted uses recorded in each certificate.

questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 19795-1:2021 (Information Technology — Biometric Performance Testing and Reporting — Part 1: Principles and Framework)
questions.question: Management is choosing between two fingerprint readers for a server room, and each vendor quotes accuracy figures at a different sensitivity setting. Which comparison basis should the IS auditor consider MOST appropriate?

options.A: The number of reference sites each vendor can name
options.B: The false acceptance rate quoted at each vendor's setting
options.C: The crossover error rate measured for each product
options.D: The image resolution listed on each product's data sheet

questions.key_concept: The crossover error rate, where false acceptance equals false rejection, is the standard basis for comparing biometric products; lower is better.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether figures quoted at different settings can be compared fairly.
questions.correct_explanation: The crossover error rate is the error rate at the setting where false acceptance and false rejection are equal (ISO/IEC 19795-1 calls it the equal error rate), so it gives one comparable accuracy figure for each product, whatever setting the vendors chose; lower is better. False acceptance rates quoted at different settings come closest: they matter, but each vendor can lower its figure by tightening its own setting, so they cannot be compared.

wrong_explanations.A: Reference sites show market use, not how accurately each reader tells genuine users from impostors.
wrong_explanations.B: Rates quoted at different settings are not comparable; either vendor could lower its figure by tightening the setting.
wrong_explanations.D: Sensor resolution is an input specification, not a measured error rate.

tips: Eliminate: A measures market presence and D a hardware specification; neither is an accuracy figure.
Final two: C beats B because the crossover rate is one comparable figure; rates quoted at different settings are not.
Exam cue: comparing biometric products overall points to the lowest crossover error rate; a concern about impostors points to false acceptance.

questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 19795-1:2021 (Information Technology — Biometric Performance Testing and Reporting — Part 1: Principles and Framework); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions.question: After staff complained of being rejected, a branch manager loosened the match threshold on the fingerprint readers guarding the cash vault. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Re-enroll every user's fingerprints to improve match quality
options.B: Recommend restoring the original threshold on every reader
options.C: Survey staff on how often the readers now reject them
options.D: Obtain the false acceptance rate at the new setting

questions.key_concept: Loosening a biometric match threshold trades fewer rejections for more false acceptances; measure that rate before concluding.
questions.pre_read: Ask which error rate rises when the match threshold is loosened.
questions.correct_explanation: Loosening the match threshold cuts false rejections but lets more impostors through. The IS auditor should first obtain the false acceptance rate at the new setting, so any finding rests on evidence of how far the vault's risk has risen. Recommending the original threshold is the closest choice: it may well be the right outcome, but recommending it before measuring the impact skips the evidence step.

wrong_explanations.A: Re-enrollment is a fix management may choose later; it does not show how much the impostor risk has risen.
wrong_explanations.B: Restoring the threshold may be the right outcome, but recommending it before measuring the impact skips the evidence step.
wrong_explanations.C: A survey measures rejections, the convenience side, not how many impostors the readers now accept.

tips: Eliminate: A jumps to a fix without measuring anything, and C measures rejections rather than impostor risk.
Final two: D beats B because the IS auditor needs evidence of the new false acceptance rate before recommending a setting.
Exam cue: when a biometric threshold is loosened to stop complaints, check false acceptance first; that is where the security risk moves.

questions.framework_ref: OASIS SAML 2.0 Core; NIST SP 800-63C-4 (Digital Identity Guidelines: Federation and Assertions)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds a web application accepts Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertions from the identity provider without checking their signatures. Which attack does this MOST LIKELY allow?

options.A: Reading assertions as they travel to the application
options.B: Locking users out by flooding the identity provider
options.C: Guessing user passwords at the identity provider's login page
options.D: Forging an assertion to sign in as any user

questions.key_concept: Applications must validate the identity provider's signature on each assertion; otherwise anyone can forge one and sign in as any user.
questions.pre_read: Ask what stops someone from writing an assertion of their own.
questions.correct_explanation: The identity provider signs each assertion so applications can confirm it is genuine and unchanged. An application that skips the check will accept an assertion anyone writes, so an attacker can claim to be any user, including an administrator, without a password. Reading assertions in transit nearly wins, but signatures never provided secrecy; that depends on encrypting the connection or the assertion.

wrong_explanations.A: Signature checks protect authenticity, not secrecy; reading assertions in transit depends on whether the connection is encrypted.
wrong_explanations.B: Flooding is an availability attack on the identity provider; it is unaffected by how the application checks signatures.
wrong_explanations.C: Password guessing targets the identity provider's login, which the application's missing signature check does not weaken.

tips: Eliminate: B and C attack the identity provider itself, which the application's missing check does not weaken.
Final two: D beats A because unchecked assertions let anyone write one; signatures never kept assertions secret.
Exam cue: in single sign-on, every application must validate the identity provider's signature, or anyone can claim any identity.

questions.subtopic: Single Sign-On. Local Logins That Bypass the Identity Provider
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63C-4 (Digital Identity Guidelines: Federation and Assertions); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions.question: After a firm moved 30 applications behind single sign-on with multi-factor authentication, each application kept its own password login as a backup. Which risk should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: Users may forget backup passwords they seldom use
options.B: One stolen password could open an application without a second factor
options.C: Local application password rules may be weaker than the firm's policy
options.D: Users may be confused by two different sign-in screens

questions.key_concept: Single sign-on protects only if every login goes through the identity provider; local backup logins skip its multi-factor authentication and deprovisioning.
questions.pre_read: Ask which controls the identity provider applies that a local password login would skip.
questions.correct_explanation: Single sign-on makes the identity provider the one front door, where multi-factor authentication is enforced and access is removed when staff leave. A password login kept on each application is a side door around both: a stolen password works without a second factor, and unless each local account is also disabled, former staff keep access. Weaker local password rules are the strongest alternative; even strong passwords still skip those controls.

wrong_explanations.A: Forgotten passwords cause help desk calls, an inconvenience rather than a security exposure.
wrong_explanations.C: Weak local rules add to the risk, but even strong backup passwords still skip the second factor and central disabling.
wrong_explanations.D: Two sign-in screens may confuse users, but confusion is a usability issue, not a control gap.

tips: Eliminate: A and D describe user inconvenience, not a way around the security controls.
Final two: B beats C because any local login, strong or weak, skips the second factor and central disabling.
Exam cue: single sign-on moves the front door to one place; any login that bypasses it must be removed or tightly controlled.

questions.subtopic: Intrusion Prevention. Who Chooses Fail Open or Fail Closed
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-94 (Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions.question: Network engineers configured the inline intrusion prevention system protecting a payment platform to fail open, so sales continue if it crashes. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Recommend switching the device to fail closed to protect security
options.B: Verify the business owner formally approved this trade-off
options.C: Recommend moving the device to a mirrored port to avoid outages
options.D: Test whether the device's attack signatures are kept up to date

questions.key_concept: An inline device's failure mode trades security against availability; the business owner decides it on assessed risk, not engineers or the IS auditor.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns a security-versus-availability trade-off before judging which setting is right.
questions.correct_explanation: Failing open keeps payments flowing but lets traffic pass uninspected while the device is down; failing closed protects but stops sales. Choosing between them is a business risk decision, so the IS auditor first verifies that the business owner made it on assessed risk. Recommending fail closed is the most tempting alternative: it may be right, but the IS auditor would be making the owner's decision without the risk basis.

wrong_explanations.A: Fail closed may be right, but it halts sales on every crash; the business owner weighs that trade-off, and the IS auditor first checks it was weighed.
wrong_explanations.C: On a mirrored port the device can only alert, so it would stop blocking attacks entirely; that removes the control instead of managing its failure.
wrong_explanations.D: Signature currency affects detection quality, but it does not show who accepted the risk of uninspected traffic during a failure.

tips: Eliminate: C turns the device into a detector that cannot block, and D checks signatures, which says nothing about the failure setting.
Final two: B beats A because the failure mode trades security against availability, a decision the business owner makes on assessed risk.
Exam cue: when technical staff have made a risk trade-off, the IS auditor first checks that the right owner made it.

questions.subtopic: Unified Threat Management. Consolidated Appliance Risk
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev 1 (Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-7 (Boundary Protection); COBIT 2019 BAI04 (Managed Availability and Capacity)
questions.question: A retailer replaced each store's separate firewall, intrusion prevention and virtual private network (VPN) devices with one unified threat management appliance, without a spare. Which risk should the IS auditor rank GREATEST?

options.A: Vendor default rule sets may not suit each store's traffic
options.B: Combined inspection could slow traffic during busy trading hours
options.C: One hardware fault could disable every security function at once
options.D: Logs from every function would be stored on one device

questions.key_concept: Consolidating controls in one appliance simplifies operation but makes it a single point of failure; critical sites need resilience.
questions.pre_read: When several controls move into one box, ask what happens to all of them when that box fails.
questions.correct_explanation: A unified threat management appliance concentrates the firewall, intrusion prevention and VPN in one device. With no spare, a single fault takes all of those controls down together, leaving the store either offline or unprotected. Slower inspection at peak comes closest: it degrades service and can be fixed by sizing or tuning, but it leaves protection running, unlike a failure.

wrong_explanations.A: Default rules need tuning to each store's traffic, a one-time setup task; it does not remove protection the way a failure of the only device does.
wrong_explanations.B: Inspection load can slow traffic, but capacity sizing fixes it, and a slowdown leaves protection in place, unlike a total failure.
wrong_explanations.D: Logs kept on the appliance are a retention issue fixed by forwarding them to a central system; the controls keep working.

tips: Eliminate: A is a one-time tuning task and D a log retention fix; neither leaves the store unprotected.
Final two: C beats B because a slowdown keeps protection running, while one fault removes every consolidated control at once.
Exam cue: consolidation trades simplicity for concentration; look for the single point of failure and ask for redundancy.

questions.subtopic: Network Access Control. Devices That Cannot Be Posture-Checked
questions.framework_ref: IEEE 802.1X (Port-Based Network Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IA-3 (Device Identification and Authentication); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-7 (Boundary Protection)
questions.question: Network access control exempts 300 printers and badge readers that cannot run its health-check agent, and they receive full network access. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Place these devices on a segment reaching only needed systems
options.B: Admit these devices once their hardware addresses are registered
options.C: Remove these devices until vendors add support for the agent
options.D: Review the exemption list with the network team every year

questions.key_concept: Devices that cannot pass a health check need compensating controls; restrict what they can reach rather than trusting identifiers that are easily copied.
questions.pre_read: When a control cannot be applied to some devices, ask what compensating control limits the harm they could cause.
questions.correct_explanation: Printers and badge readers that skip the health check are a gap in network access control, and full access lets anyone who impersonates one reach the whole network. A restricted segment that reaches only their print and badge servers compensates for the missing check. Registering hardware addresses is the closest choice: it identifies the devices, but addresses are easily copied, so an impostor would still get full access.

wrong_explanations.B: Registration does inventory which printers and readers belong, yet a cloned address passes it; when devices cannot prove health, limit their reach.
wrong_explanations.C: Taking printers and badge readers offline would disrupt operations; a compensating control can limit the risk without removing needed devices.
wrong_explanations.D: A yearly review checks who is exempt but leaves the exempt devices with full network access all year.

tips: Eliminate: C removes devices the business needs, and D only reviews the exemption list while full access continues.
Final two: A beats B because copied hardware addresses defeat registration, while a restricted segment limits what any impostor reaches.
Exam cue: when a preventive check cannot be applied, look for the compensating control that limits impact, not just identification.

questions.subtopic: Firewall Rule Sets. Rule Base Approach
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev 1 (Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy); COBIT 2019 DSS05 (Managed Security Services)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds a broad allow rule near the top of a first-match perimeter firewall's rule set, above deny rules for known malicious networks. Which risk is MOST significant?

options.A: Firewall throughput may fall as each packet meets more rules
options.B: Administrators may find the out-of-order rule set harder to maintain
options.C: Legitimate traffic may be blocked by the overlapping deny rules
options.D: Malicious traffic is allowed before any deny rule is reached

questions.key_concept: First-match firewalls apply rules in order, so a broad allow rule placed above deny rules makes those deny rules useless.
questions.pre_read: Notice the firewall stops at the first rule that matches. Ask which rule malicious traffic meets first.
questions.correct_explanation: A first-match firewall stops at the first rule a packet matches. Traffic from the malicious networks hits the broad allow rule first, so the deny rules below it never apply and the protection exists only on paper. An out-of-order rule set is also harder to maintain, which makes that option the closest choice, but that is an administrative weakness, while the misplaced allow rule lets hostile traffic in now.

wrong_explanations.A: Rule count can affect performance slightly, but the real problem is which rule matches first, not how many are checked.
wrong_explanations.B: Poor ordering does make review harder, but the immediate harm is that the deny rules never fire against malicious traffic.
wrong_explanations.C: A broad allow rule above the deny rules lets traffic in; it does not cause legitimate traffic to be blocked.

tips: Eliminate: A is a performance concern, and C reverses the effect; a broad allow rule admits traffic rather than blocking it.
Final two: D beats B because the misplaced allow rule admits hostile traffic now, while harder maintenance is an administrative weakness.
Exam cue: in first-match rule sets, order is security; specific deny rules must sit above broad allow rules.

questions.subtopic: Firewall Rule Sets. Rule Base Approach
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev 1 (Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-7(5) (Deny by Default — Allow by Exception)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds a manufacturer's internet firewall blocks a list of known malicious ports and allows all other inbound traffic. What is the PRIMARY weakness of this approach?

options.A: Unlisted services stay reachable by anyone outside the company
options.B: The block list needs frequent updates as new threats appear
options.C: Checking each packet against a long list may slow traffic
options.D: Outbound traffic from staff computers is not being filtered

questions.key_concept: Firewall rule sets should deny by default and allow only approved traffic; a block list leaves every unlisted service exposed.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens to traffic the rules never mention; that default decides the firewall's real strength.
questions.correct_explanation: A block list is a default-allow stance: anything not listed passes, so a new service, a forgotten test server or an unusual port is open to outsiders. Default deny reverses this, allowing only approved traffic. Constant list updates nearly win: they are a real burden, but even a perfectly current list still exposes every service nobody thought to block.

wrong_explanations.B: Keeping the list current is a burden, but even a perfect list leaves every unlisted service exposed; the default-allow stance is the flaw.
wrong_explanations.C: Rule matching on modern firewalls adds little delay; speed is not the control weakness in a default-allow rule set.
wrong_explanations.D: The finding concerns inbound rules; nothing in it shows outbound traffic is unfiltered, so this weakness is not established.

tips: Eliminate: C worries about speed rather than exposure, and D assumes an outbound gap the finding never shows.
Final two: A beats B because the update burden is a symptom; default allow exposes unlisted services even when the list is current.
Exam cue: for any firewall rule set, check the default first; deny by default with approved exceptions is the expected stance.

questions.subtopic: Firewall Types. Firewall Types for Return Traffic
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev 1 (Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy)
questions.question: A branch router's static packet filter allows all inbound traffic to high-numbered ports so that replies to staff web sessions get through. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Limit the open range to the reply ports client systems use
options.B: Use stateful inspection that tracks inside connections
options.C: Log each inbound connection that reaches the open high ports
options.D: Scan the branch's internal hosts for vulnerabilities each month

questions.key_concept: Stateful firewalls track connections and admit only replies to sessions started inside; static packet filters must leave reply ports open to everyone.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the device remembers which conversations started inside, or must trust any packet arriving on an allowed port.
questions.correct_explanation: A static packet filter judges each packet alone, so to let replies in it must open the high ports to anyone, and outsiders can reach any internal service listening there. Stateful inspection records connections started from inside and admits only their replies. Narrowing the range is the strongest alternative: it shrinks the opening, but thousands of ports stay open to unsolicited traffic.

wrong_explanations.A: Like stateful inspection, a narrower range aims to admit only replies. But port numbers cannot tell replies from attacks; connection tracking can.
wrong_explanations.C: Logging records connections through the opening after the fact; it does not stop outsiders from using it.
wrong_explanations.D: Monthly scans may find weak internal hosts, but the open inbound ports still let outsiders reach them between scans.

tips: Eliminate: C and D detect problems after the fact and leave the inbound opening in place.
Final two: B beats A because tracking connections admits replies alone, while a narrower range still accepts unsolicited traffic.
Exam cue: when a filter must open ports broadly to let replies in, the fix is stateful inspection, not a smaller hole.

questions.subtopic: Enterprise Wireless. Personal Devices on the Corporate Network
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-153 (Guidelines for Securing WLANs); IEEE 802.1X (Port-Based Network Access Control)
questions.question: Policy permits only corporate-controlled devices on the internal network, yet staff join personal phones to the corporate wireless, which reaches file servers, using directory passwords. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Register approved devices by their hardware addresses on the controller
options.B: Require staff to change their directory passwords more often
options.C: Turn off the network's broadcast so personal phones cannot see it
options.D: Admit company-managed devices that present an issued device certificate

questions.key_concept: Password-based enterprise wireless proves who the user is, not which device connects; device certificates limit access to managed equipment.
questions.pre_read: Separate the two questions an access control can answer: who is connecting, and from what device.
questions.correct_explanation: Directory passwords prove who the user is but say nothing about the device, so unmanaged phones of unknown security reach internal file servers. Issuing certificates to company-managed devices and requiring one to connect keeps unmanaged equipment off that network; personal phones can use a separate one. Registering hardware addresses is the most tempting alternative: it looks similar, but addresses are easily copied and cannot prove a device is managed.

wrong_explanations.A: An auditor would see address registration as progress toward device control. But addresses copy easily; trust needs a credential bound to the device.
wrong_explanations.B: More frequent password changes do not stop staff from entering a valid password on an unmanaged phone.
wrong_explanations.C: Stopping the broadcast hides little: devices reveal the network name when they connect, and staff who know it can still join from personal phones.

tips: Eliminate: B changes passwords that staff can still enter on any phone, and C stops a broadcast, though devices reveal the name when they connect.
Final two: D beats A because a certificate kept on managed devices is far harder to copy than a hardware address.
Exam cue: where only managed devices are allowed, user passwords cannot enforce it; require a device identity tied to management.

questions.subtopic: Wireless Encryption. Legacy WEP Devices Awaiting Replacement
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-97 (Establishing Wireless Robust Security Networks: A Guide to IEEE 802.11i); NIST SP 800-153 (Guidelines for Securing WLANs)
questions.question: A distribution center's handheld scanners support only Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP), and approved replacements arrive in nine months. Which interim measure should the IS auditor consider MOST appropriate?

options.A: Change the WEP key every week until the replacements arrive
options.B: Limit the scanner network to reaching the inventory server alone
options.C: Hide the scanner network's name from public broadcast
options.D: Require scanner operators to change their sign-in passwords monthly

questions.key_concept: When a broken protocol must stay in use for a while, contain it: restrict what the weak network can reach until it is replaced.
questions.pre_read: If the weak control cannot be fixed yet, ask which measure limits the damage when it is broken.
questions.correct_explanation: WEP keys can be recovered from captured traffic in minutes, so anyone nearby could join the scanner network. Limiting that network to the inventory server means an intruder reaches one system instead of the corporate network, while management accepts the remaining risk until replacement. Weekly key changes come closest: they feel active, but a key cracked in minutes protects for almost none of the week.

wrong_explanations.A: When encryption is broken, contain what an intruder can reach. Key rotation suits intact ciphers, but it cannot rescue one already broken.
wrong_explanations.C: Hidden network names are revealed whenever devices connect, so hiding this one does not stop anyone from cracking the WEP key.
wrong_explanations.D: Scanner sign-in passwords protect the handheld application, not the radio link; an outsider can still break WEP and join the network.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on a hidden name that connecting devices reveal, and D changes application passwords that do nothing for the radio link.
Final two: B beats A because a key cracked in minutes defeats weekly changes, while restriction limits what an intruder reaches.
Exam cue: when a weak control must stay for now, prefer a compensating control that limits impact over cosmetic hardening.

questions.subtopic: Rogue Access Points. Preventing Rogue Access Points
questions.framework_ref: IEEE 802.1X (Port-Based Network Access Control); NIST SP 800-153 (Guidelines for Securing WLANs)
questions.question: An IS auditor's site survey found two consumer access points staff had plugged into meeting-room network jacks to boost signal. Which control would MOST LIKELY have prevented this?

options.A: A wireless intrusion detection system with alerts sent to an owner
options.B: An acceptable use policy that bans personal network equipment
options.C: Device authentication enforced at every wired switch port
options.D: Quarterly wireless site surveys of every office floor

questions.key_concept: Port-based authentication on wired switch ports stops unapproved access points from connecting; wireless monitoring only finds them afterward.
questions.pre_read: Note whether the stem asks to prevent, detect or correct, then pick the control type that matches.
questions.correct_explanation: Port-based authentication, such as 802.1X, lets a wired port carry traffic only after the connected device proves it is approved. A consumer access point has no credentials, so the port stays closed and the device never bridges into the network. Wireless intrusion detection is the closest choice: with an owner acting on alerts it finds rogue devices quickly, but only after they are already connected.

wrong_explanations.A: Wireless intrusion detection finds rogue access points once they are live; even with prompt alerts, it detects the connection rather than preventing it.
wrong_explanations.B: A policy states the rule, but staff who wanted a better signal could still plug a device into an open port.
wrong_explanations.D: Surveys every quarter detect rogue devices after the fact and could leave one connected for months.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on staff obeying a rule, and D finds devices only at the next quarterly visit.
Final two: C beats A because port authentication blocks the device from connecting, while intrusion detection reports it afterward.
Exam cue: when the stem asks what would have prevented an event, choose the preventive control over strong detective ones.

questions.subtopic: Rogue Access Points. Evidence That None Exist
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-153 (Guidelines for Securing WLANs); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions.question: An IS auditor must conclude whether unapproved wireless access points are operating at 30 branch offices. Which evidence would be MOST reliable?

options.A: Recent radio scans of every branch, tracing each unknown device
options.B: The network team's current inventory of approved access points
options.C: A copy of the signed policy banning unapproved wireless devices
options.D: Signed statements from every branch manager that none are present

questions.key_concept: Rogue devices are, by definition, missing from approved inventories; direct radio scanning, with follow-up, shows whether they exist.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the evidence source could ever contain the thing you are looking for.
questions.correct_explanation: Unapproved access points are, by definition, absent from the network team's records, so the reliable way to find them is to examine the airwaves. Recent radio scans at every branch, with each unknown device traced to its source, give direct, independent evidence. The approved inventory nearly wins: it is accurate for managed devices, but it cannot show devices nobody registered.

wrong_explanations.B: An auditor would rely on the approved inventory for approved devices. Rogue ones are absent by definition: search the environment itself for the unrecorded.
wrong_explanations.C: A policy shows what is required, not what is happening; it gives no evidence that branches comply.
wrong_explanations.D: Manager statements are indirect testimony; a manager may not know that a staff member plugged in a device.

tips: Eliminate: C shows a requirement rather than compliance, and D relies on managers' statements instead of direct observation.
Final two: A beats B because an inventory of approved devices can never list the unapproved ones the scans find.
Exam cue: the most reliable evidence is direct and independent; ask whether the source could even contain the problem.

questions.subtopic: Fire Suppression. Choosing a Water-Based Design
questions.framework_ref: NFPA 75 (Standard for the Fire Protection of Information Technology Equipment); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-13 (Fire Protection)
questions.question: Local fire code requires a water-based suppression system in a new data center, and management's main concern is accidental discharge onto servers. Which design should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Pipes kept full of water that sprays when heat opens a head
options.B: Pipes holding pressurized air that fill once any head opens
options.C: Dry pipes that fill on a detector alarm, spraying where heads open
options.D: Open heads across the room that spray together once detectors trigger

questions.key_concept: Where water suppression is required near IT equipment, pre-action designs need both detection and an opened head before water is released.
questions.pre_read: For each design, count how many separate failures it would take for water to reach equipment.
questions.correct_explanation: A pre-action system keeps its pipes dry until detectors sense a fire, and water flows only when a heat-opened head follows, so a knocked head or a false alarm alone releases nothing. A conventional dry-pipe system is the strongest alternative: its pipes also hold no water, but it is built for freezing spaces, and one damaged head lets the air out and water in.

wrong_explanations.A: Wet-pipe systems hold water at all times, so a leaking joint or a knocked head soaks equipment immediately.
wrong_explanations.B: Dry-pipe systems suit freezing areas; one damaged head lets the air out and water flows, so a single accident still causes discharge.
wrong_explanations.D: Deluge systems spray from every open head at once when detection triggers, flooding the whole room even for a small fire.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps water in the pipes permanently, and D sprays the whole room from open heads at once.
Final two: C beats B because pre-action needs a detector alarm and an opened head, while dry pipe discharges after one knocked head.
Exam cue: ISACA sometimes calls pre-action 'dry pipe'; judge by mechanism: choose the design that needs a detector alarm before water enters the pipes.

questions.framework_ref: NFPA 2001 (Standard on Clean Agent Fire Extinguishing Systems); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-13 (Fire Protection)
questions.question: A server room protected by clean-agent gas suppression had cable holes cut through its walls during a recent upgrade, and they were never sealed. Which risk should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: Gas escaping through the holes could harm staff in nearby offices
options.B: Dust drawn in through the openings could clog the servers' cooling fans
options.C: Humidity in the room could drift outside the range servers need
options.D: Leaks could drop the concentration below what stops a fire

questions.key_concept: Clean-agent suppression works only if the room holds the gas at extinguishing concentration; unsealed openings let it leak before the fire is out.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a control needs from its surroundings to work, and whether a recent change has taken that away.
questions.correct_explanation: Clean-agent systems put out fire by holding a set gas concentration in a sealed room for several minutes. Unsealed cable holes let the gas leak away, so the fire may not go out or may reignite; the room needs resealing and an integrity test. Harm to staff nearby is the most tempting alternative: these agents are chosen to be safe at the planned level, and escaping gas only becomes more diluted.

wrong_explanations.A: Clean agents are chosen to be safe for people at the planned concentration, and gas escaping into larger offices becomes even more diluted.
wrong_explanations.B: Dust is a housekeeping concern that filters and cleaning manage; it does not stop the suppression system from working in a fire.
wrong_explanations.C: Humidity control is a separate environmental issue; small cable holes barely affect it and do not disable fire protection.

tips: Eliminate: B and C are routine environmental upkeep issues that do not stop the suppression system from working.
Final two: D beats A because clean agents are safe for people at design levels, while leaks can leave a fire burning.
Exam cue: after any change to a protected room, ask whether the control still has what it needs to work.
