questions.subtopic: Zero Trust Network Access. Limiting a Compromised Device
questions.question: A firm is replacing its virtual private network (VPN) with zero trust network access (ZTNA). Which ZTNA feature would the IS auditor expect to MOST limit harm from a compromised laptop?

options.A: Stronger encryption of the tunnel between the laptop and broker
options.B: A device health check each time a session begins
options.C: Connections only to the applications policy allows that user
options.D: One sign-on page that opens each remote application

questions.key_concept: ZTNA connects a verified user and device only to the applications policy allows, so a compromised device cannot reach the wider network.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an attacker on a compromised device could reach under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: ZTNA's main gain over a VPN is limited reach: the broker connects a user only to the applications policy allows, so a compromised laptop cannot scan or spread across the network. A device health check comes closest: it helps keep unhealthy devices out, but it can miss a compromise that has not yet been detected, while limiting reach caps the harm either way.

wrong_explanations.A: A VPN tunnel is already encrypted; stronger encryption protects data in transit but does not limit what a compromised laptop can reach.
wrong_explanations.B: Health checks block devices known to be unhealthy, but an undetected compromise passes them; limiting reach still caps the harm.
wrong_explanations.D: A single sign-on page is a convenience; it does not narrow what a compromised laptop can reach and may widen it.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because tunnel encryption and single sign-on do not limit what a compromised laptop can reach.
Final two: C beats B because health checks can miss an undetected compromise, while per-application access caps the harm either way.
Exam cue: judge remote access by what a connected device can reach, not by how strong the tunnel is.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)

Public sources: NIST.

questions.subtopic: Zero Trust Network Access. Verifying an Exposure Claim
questions.question: After a zero trust network access (ZTNA) rollout, management states its application servers can no longer be reached from the internet. Which evidence would BEST allow the IS auditor to verify this claim?

options.A: Broker logs listing each allowed and denied application session
options.B: An external scan showing the servers accept no inbound connections
options.C: The approved design stating applications connect outward to the broker
options.D: The ZTNA vendor's certificate of alignment with zero trust principles

questions.key_concept: In common ZTNA designs, applications connect outward to the broker; an external scan proves they accept no inbound internet connections.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each piece of evidence shows the intended setup or tests what is actually reachable today.
questions.correct_explanation: An external scan tests the claim directly: if the servers accept no inbound connections from the internet, they are hidden behind the broker in practice. The approved design is the closest choice: it shows the intended setup, but a leftover firewall rule or old remote-access path could still expose a server, and only a test of the live state would reveal it.

wrong_explanations.A: Broker logs show decisions on traffic that passes through the broker; they cannot show whether servers are also reachable by another path.
wrong_explanations.C: A design shows what was intended; a leftover firewall rule or old access path could still expose servers despite it.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor certificate speaks to the product in general, not to how this organization configured its own servers.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because broker logs only see traffic through the broker and a vendor certificate covers the product, not this setup.
Final two: B beats C because a design shows intent, while a scan of the live servers shows they really are hidden.
Exam cue: when management claims a control works, prefer evidence that tests the live result over documents describing the plan.

Distinct from d5_050 and d5_286 (zero trust access decisions): tests which evidence proves applications are hidden from the internet after a ZTNA rollout. Public sources: NIST.

questions.question: A bank built the cryptographic inventory for its post-quantum migration from questionnaires that system owners completed. Which procedure should the IS auditor use to BEST test its completeness?

options.A: Have each system owner confirm their entries in writing
options.B: Check that every entry records the algorithm and key length
options.C: Trace a sample of inventory entries to the systems they name
options.D: Compare the inventory with a discovery scan of live systems

questions.key_concept: Test completeness by starting from an independent source, such as a discovery scan of live systems, and looking for items the inventory lacks.
questions.pre_read: Ask which direction each test runs: from the record to reality, or from reality to the record.
questions.correct_explanation: Completeness means finding what the questionnaires missed, so the test must start from an independent view of what really exists, such as a discovery scan of live systems, and look for algorithms the inventory lacks. Tracing sampled entries to their systems nearly wins: it confirms that listed items are real and accurate, but it starts from the inventory, so it cannot reveal anything left out.

wrong_explanations.A: Owners who missed a system in the questionnaire are likely to miss it again; their sign-off adds no independent view of what exists.
wrong_explanations.B: Checking each entry's fields shows the listed items are well described, not that unlisted systems are missing.
wrong_explanations.C: Tracing from the inventory confirms listed entries exist and are accurate, but anything never listed is never sampled.

tips: Eliminate: A and B, because owners re-confirming repeats the same source, and checking entry fields says nothing about missing systems.
Final two: D beats C because completeness is tested from live systems toward the list; tracing listed entries cannot find omissions.
Exam cue: to test completeness, start from an independent population and look for items missing from the record.

questions.subtopic: Post-Quantum Cryptography. Interim Response to the Quantum Threat
questions.question: To prepare for quantum computers, an IT manager plans to double the key length of all Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA) certificates used to sign long-term contracts. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: A capable quantum computer breaks RSA at any practical key length
options.B: Longer RSA keys will slow signing and checking on older devices
options.C: Quantum attacks will also break symmetric 256-bit contract encryption
options.D: Certificates with longer RSA keys will cost more to renew each year

questions.key_concept: Quantum computers break RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography at any practical key length; the answer is standardized post-quantum algorithms, not longer keys.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the proposed change works against the stated threat before weighing its side effects.
questions.correct_explanation: A large quantum computer breaks RSA with Shor's algorithm, whose cost grows only modestly with key length, so longer keys buy no lasting protection. Signatures on long-term contracts must stay trustworthy for decades, so they need a standardized post-quantum signature algorithm. Slower signing on older devices is the strongest alternative: it is a real cost, but a manageable one beside a change that fails against the threat.

wrong_explanations.B: Slower processing is an operating cost the organization can manage; it matters less than a change that fails against the quantum threat itself.
wrong_explanations.C: 256-bit symmetric encryption is expected to stay strong against quantum attack; the urgent exposure is public-key cryptography such as RSA.
wrong_explanations.D: Certificate fees rarely depend on key length, and even a higher fee would be minor beside a control that fails.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because 256-bit symmetric encryption stays strong and certificate fees are a minor cost, not a security concern.
Final two: A beats B because slower signing is a manageable cost, while longer RSA keys give no lasting protection against quantum attack.
Exam cue: rank a weak remedy by whether it works against the threat before weighing its side effects.

Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 5A6.6 (batch Q16: practice for the web v12.24 study notes). Distinct from d5_074 (migration order), d5_079 (inventory first), d5_249 (crypto-agility) and d2_174 (stalled migration governance): tests why longer RSA keys are not an answer to the quantum threat. The same misconception appears as d5_249 option D ('use longer RSA keys until the standards settle'); this item builds a full question on it, matching the 5A6.6 exam trap. Public sources: NIST and ISO.

questions.subtopic: Serverless Functions. Reach of a Flawed Function
questions.question: An IS auditor learns an attacker exploited a company's receipt-formatting serverless function, then deleted records in its own human resources (HR) database. What MOST likely explains how the function reached HR data?

options.A: The function did not validate the event data it received
options.B: The provider failed to isolate one customer's functions from another's
options.C: The HR database was not encrypted at rest
options.D: Functions shared one execution role with wide database rights

questions.key_concept: Each serverless function runs under an execution role; one shared, over-broad role lets a single flawed function reach everything.
questions.pre_read: Separate how the attacker got in from what the compromised component was allowed to reach.
questions.correct_explanation: Each function acts with the rights of its execution role. If all functions share one role with wide database rights, a flaw in any function, even a receipt formatter, reaches everything those rights allow. Missing event validation is the most tempting alternative: it may explain how the attacker got into the function, but not why that function could touch HR data; a least-privilege role would have contained it.

wrong_explanations.A: Unvalidated event data may explain how the attacker entered the function; its reach into HR data came from the rights it ran with.
wrong_explanations.B: Provider isolation separates different customers; here the function and the HR database belong to the same customer, whose permissions decided the reach.
wrong_explanations.C: Encryption at rest protects stored files from theft; a function acting through an authorized role sees the data in clear text anyway.

tips: Eliminate: B and C, because provider isolation separates different customers, and encryption at rest does not stop an authorized role.
Final two: D beats A because missing validation explains the entry, while the shared role explains why one function could reach HR data.
Exam cue: when a small component causes wide damage, look for the over-broad permissions behind it, not only the flaw used to get in.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Serverless Functions. Reach of a Flawed Function'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 5A8.6 (batch Q16: practice for the web v12.24 study notes). Distinct from the D5 cloud shared-responsibility items: tests why one flawed serverless function could reach unrelated data through a shared execution role. Public sources: NIST and ISACA.

questions.question: A bot triggered a public serverless function millions of times overnight, running up a large cloud bill before anyone noticed. Which control should the IS auditor recommend as BEST to contain a repeat?

options.A: Spending alerts that notify the cloud team when costs spike
options.B: Concurrency limits that cap how many instances run at once
options.C: A larger cloud budget reserved for unexpected usage spikes
options.D: Faster automatic scaling so the function keeps up with demand

questions.key_concept: Denial of wallet floods functions to run up costs; concurrency limits cap how fast costs can grow, and spending alerts act as a backstop.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each option limits the harm automatically or depends on someone noticing it and acting.
questions.correct_explanation: Concurrency limits cap how many instances of the function can run at once, so a flood of triggers can only run up the bill at a capped rate. This attack, called denial of wallet, needs a preventive cap. Spending alerts come closest: they flag the spike sooner than any log review, but overnight nobody may act before costs pile up, so they back up the cap rather than replace it.

wrong_explanations.A: Spending alerts flag the flood quickly, but someone must still act on them, and overnight the bill keeps growing until they do.
wrong_explanations.C: A bigger budget absorbs the cost instead of limiting it, and lets an attacker run the bill even higher.
wrong_explanations.D: Faster scaling lets more instances run at once, so the same bot attack would cost even more.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because a bigger budget absorbs the cost and faster scaling lets the attack run up even more.
Final two: B beats A because a concurrency cap limits runaway costs automatically, while a spending alert still needs someone to act.
Exam cue: when harm grows by the minute, prefer a control that caps it automatically over one that reports it later.

questions.question: Hotel staff open guest room doors by holding an enrolled phone near the lock using near-field communication (NFC), even while the phone is locked. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Require a deliberate action on the phone for each opening
options.B: Log every door opening and review the logs each week
options.C: Reduce the lock reader's range to under one centimeter
options.D: Encrypt the credential each phone sends to the lock

questions.key_concept: Proximity alone does not prove presence: relay attacks forward signals, so each tap or opening needs a deliberate user action.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the option stops a misuse when it happens or only records it for later.
questions.correct_explanation: With no action on the phone, a lost phone opens any enrolled door, and a relay attack can forward a staff member's phone signal to a distant lock while the holder is elsewhere. A deliberate unlock or confirmation for each opening stops both. Weekly log review is the closest choice: logs help investigate, but they record a relayed opening only after the guest's room was entered.

wrong_explanations.B: Logs show which phone opened a door, but a relayed opening looks legitimate and is found only after the room was entered.
wrong_explanations.C: A relay attack forwards the signal over any distance, so a shorter reader range does not prove the phone is really present.
wrong_explanations.D: A relay forwards the encrypted exchange unchanged, so the lock still accepts it; encryption stops eavesdropping, not relaying.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because a relay forwards the signal over any distance and passes an encrypted exchange through unchanged.
Final two: A beats B because a deliberate action stops a relayed opening, while log review finds it only after the room was entered.
Exam cue: short range is not a security control; look for a deliberate user action at each transaction.

questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Near-Field Communication. Phone-Based Door Access'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 5A9.5 (batch Q16: practice for the web v12.24 study notes). questions.subtopic: Bluetooth Security. Judging a Remediation Claim
questions.question: To close a finding on unpatched firmware in staff Bluetooth headsets, management turned off Bluetooth discoverability on all company phones. Which reason should MOST lead the IS auditor to doubt the finding is resolved?

options.A: Staff can switch discoverability back on in their phone settings
options.B: The change was made without a record in the change log
options.C: The change leaves the vulnerable headsets exactly as they were
options.D: Attackers with antennas can reach Bluetooth devices from far away

questions.key_concept: Turning off Bluetooth discoverability only hides devices from casual scans; patching and confirmed pairing address the actual flaws.
questions.pre_read: Compare the fix with the cause named in the finding: does it remove the cause, or only reduce exposure?
questions.correct_explanation: The finding is about flaws in the headsets' firmware, and only patching removes them. Hiding the phones treats the exposure, not the cause: the headsets themselves are untouched, and a hidden device's address can still be learned from its traffic. Staff switching discoverability back on nearly wins: enforcing the setting through device management would help, yet the flaws would still be there.

wrong_explanations.A: Enforcing the setting through device management would close this gap, but even an enforced hidden mode leaves the headsets' firmware flaws in place.
wrong_explanations.B: A missing change record is a process gap worth noting, but it does not show whether the headsets' flaws were fixed.
wrong_explanations.D: Antennas extend Bluetooth range, but range is not what the finding is about; the headsets' unpatched flaws are the issue either way.

tips: Eliminate: B and D, because a missing change record and Bluetooth's range say nothing about whether the headsets' flaws were fixed.
Final two: C beats A because even an enforced hidden setting leaves the firmware flaws; only patching removes the cause.
Exam cue: check that a fix addresses the cause named in the finding, not just one way it could be exposed.

questions.question: Management proposes extending central log retention from 14 to 90 days to support investigations of advanced persistent threats (APTs). Which recommendation should the IS auditor make as BEST?

options.A: Extend central log retention to at least one year
options.B: Accept 90 days and forward host logs in real time
options.C: Accept 90 days and tune alerts to detect intrusions sooner
options.D: Keep one year of logs on each host instead of centrally

questions.key_concept: APTs often stay hidden for months, so retention must cover that dwell time, typically about a year; 90 days can still miss the start.
questions.pre_read: Compare the proposed retention with how long this kind of attacker usually stays unnoticed.
questions.correct_explanation: An advanced persistent threat often stays hidden for months; its dwell time (how long an intruder goes unnoticed) can exceed 90 days. Logs must reach back to the intrusion's start, so the auditor recommends at least a year of central retention. Real-time forwarding is the tempting option: it stops attackers deleting host logs, but with 90 days kept, the early history is still gone when the APT is found.

wrong_explanations.B: Real-time forwarding protects host logs from deletion, but 90 days of central history can still end before the intrusion began.
wrong_explanations.C: Faster alerting may shorten future dwell time, but investigators still lack history for an intrusion that began months ago.
wrong_explanations.D: An intruder with administrator rights can wipe logs kept on the hosts it controls; long history must sit centrally, out of the attacker's reach.

tips: Eliminate: C improves detection without keeping history, and D keeps a year only on hosts an intruder can wipe.
Final two: A beats B because APTs hide for months; real-time forwarding stops deletion, but 90 days may still miss the start.
Exam cue: when an APT appears in the stem, think months of hidden presence; a control measured in days or weeks will miss it.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds a company manages vulnerabilities only by scanning monthly and applying vendor patches. What is the PRIMARY reason this process fails against zero-day exploits?

options.A: Zero-day exploits target systems that skipped older patches
options.B: A monthly scanning cycle leaves vendor-patched flaws open for several weeks
options.C: No vendor patch or scanner check exists yet for such flaws
options.D: Scans rank flaws by severity score, not by active exploitation

questions.key_concept: A zero-day exploit attacks a flaw with no patch yet and often no scanner check, so scan-and-patch cannot see or close it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a scanner and a vendor patch both need to exist before either can help.
questions.correct_explanation: A zero-day exploit attacks a flaw before its vendor has released a patch, often before anyone else knows of it. Scanners need a published check and patching needs a fix, so a scan-and-patch program cannot see or close the gap; compensating controls and reduced exposure must cover it. A slow monthly cycle is a real weakness, but it concerns known flaws, and a faster cycle would still miss a zero-day.

wrong_explanations.A: Systems missing older, available patches face known exploits, which patching does address; a zero-day targets a flaw with no patch yet.
wrong_explanations.B: A monthly cycle does leave known flaws open, but a faster cycle would still miss a flaw that has no patch or scanner check.
wrong_explanations.D: Ranking by active exploitation improves the patch order for known flaws, but a zero-day has no patch to rank or apply.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because flaws on unpatched systems are known flaws, and better ranking still needs a known flaw to rank.
Final two: C beats B because a faster cycle still cannot apply a patch that does not exist yet; zero-days fall outside scan-and-patch.
Exam cue: zero-day means no patch yet and often no scanner check; look for compensating controls or reduced exposure, not faster patching.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-40 Rev 4 (Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning)

Tests what a zero-day is and why a scan-and-patch program cannot cover it; distinct from d5_137, which asks for the live compensating control. Public sources: NIST and ISACA. questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a design that relies on containers to separate a payment service from a public website on the same server. What is the PRIMARY weakness of this separation?

options.A: Containers cannot be given separate network access rules
options.B: Shared base images could carry the same flaws into both
options.C: Containers cannot be watched for unusual activity while running
options.D: Both share one host kernel, which a flaw can breach

questions.key_concept: Containers share the host's operating system kernel, so their separation is thinner than between virtual machines; one kernel flaw can cross it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the two containers have in common underneath, and whether a flaw there could reach both.
questions.correct_explanation: Containers share the host's operating system kernel instead of each running its own, so their isolation is thinner than that of virtual machines. A kernel flaw or a privileged container lets an attacker escape from the public website to the host and reach the payment service. Shared vulnerable base images are a real risk, but pipeline scanning addresses them, and they do not explain why the boundary itself is weak.

wrong_explanations.A: Container platforms support per-container network policies, so separate access rules are possible; the weakness lies in the shared kernel underneath.
wrong_explanations.B: Vulnerable base images matter, but pipeline scanning addresses them; even clean images still share one kernel that a single flaw can breach.
wrong_explanations.C: Runtime monitoring tools watch container behavior, and detection would not strengthen the boundary between the two services anyway.

tips: Eliminate: A and C, because containers can have their own network policies and can be monitored while running.
Final two: D beats B because image scanning handles shared flaws, while the shared kernel makes the boundary itself thin.
Exam cue: containers share a kernel and virtual machines do not; for high-value separation, question container-only isolation.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-190 (Application Container Security Guide)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Container Security. Isolation Model'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 5A8.4 (batch Q17: concept practice for a subtopic previously practised only as live-incident FIRST calls or recommendations). Tests the container isolation model (shared kernel) rather than a response to an escape; distinct from d5_098 and d5_266. Public sources: NIST and ISACA.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds a Kubernetes control plane reachable from the internet, with every administrator using one shared certificate. What is the GREATEST risk of this setup?

options.A: Shared certificates make administrator actions impossible to trace to a person
options.B: Anyone holding the certificate could control every container and secret
options.C: Internet traffic to the control plane slows container scheduling
options.D: Certificates expire, which stops the cluster's containers from running

questions.key_concept: The orchestrator's control plane commands every container and holds its secrets, so exposed, shared admin access puts the whole cluster at stake.
questions.pre_read: Ask what someone holding that one credential could do across the cluster.
questions.correct_explanation: The control plane is the orchestrator's command center: it deploys and changes every container and stores the cluster's secrets. Reachable from the internet with one shared certificate, a single leaked copy hands an attacker the whole cluster, and Kubernetes cannot revoke one client certificate without reissuing them all. Lost individual accountability is a real weakness, but it limits tracing after the fact; takeover of every workload is the greater exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: A shared certificate does weaken accountability, but untraceable actions matter less than an outsider gaining control of every workload.
wrong_explanations.C: Scheduling speed is a performance matter; internet exposure is a concern because of who can reach the control plane, not how fast it responds.
wrong_explanations.D: Certificate expiry is managed by renewal and does not stop running containers; it does not explain the exposure here.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because scheduling speed and certificate renewal are operational matters, not the security exposure here.
Final two: B beats A because lost accountability limits tracing, while one leaked certificate gives an attacker control of the whole cluster.
Exam cue: treat the host and the orchestrator as crown jewels; weak access there puts every workload they manage at risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-190 (Application Container Security Guide); NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guide

Tests what the orchestrator's control plane does and why its exposure outweighs other findings; no other D5 item covers control-plane access. Public sources: NIST, NSA and CISA.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds a company's vulnerability scans cover only devices recorded in its asset register. What is the MOST likely reason this leaves its Internet of Things (IoT) devices exposed?

options.A: IoT devices encrypt their traffic, which hides them from scanners
options.B: Many IoT devices cannot be patched even when flaws are found
options.C: Teams often buy and connect these devices without informing IT
options.D: Scanners are built to assess desktop operating systems, not embedded devices

questions.key_concept: IoT devices are often bought and connected outside IT, so they are missing from the asset register, and anything driven by it skips them.
questions.pre_read: Notice what decides which devices get scanned, then ask which devices are least likely to be on that list.
questions.correct_explanation: IoT devices such as cameras, sensors and building controls are often bought by facilities or business teams and connected without IT's knowledge, so they never reach the asset register. Scans driven by that register skip them, leaving their flaws unseen. That many devices cannot be patched is a real problem, but it arises only after a flaw is found; here the devices are never examined at all.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption protects the content of traffic; a scanner still finds and probes the device on the network if it is told to look.
wrong_explanations.B: Patching limits matter after a flaw is found; here the devices are never scanned, so their flaws are never found in the first place.
wrong_explanations.D: Vulnerability scanners assess network devices, appliances and embedded systems as well as computers; the gap is which devices they are pointed at.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because a scanner finds a device whether or not its traffic is encrypted, and scanners assess embedded devices too.
Final two: C beats B because the stem says scans follow the register; unlisted devices are never examined, before patching even arises.
Exam cue: devices nobody knows about cannot be protected; when a control works from a list, ask what is missing from the list.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8 Control 1 (Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets); NIST SP 800-213 (IoT Device Cybersecurity Guidance for the Federal Government)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IoT Security. Asset Visibility'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 5A9.4 (batch Q17: concept practice for a subtopic previously practised only as live-incident FIRST calls or recommendations). Tests why IoT devices escape IT controls (they are invisible to IT); distinct from d5_241, which recommends building the inventory. Public sources: NIST, CIS and ISACA. D5 difficulty upgrade (Oct 2026, owner's rule: eliminations fall to CISA knowledge, final two decided by the ISACA lens): Eliminate tip no longer says 'hide'.

questions.question: Sampling supplier bank-detail changes, an IS auditor finds each was confirmed by calling the phone number given in the change request. What is the PRIMARY weakness in this control?

options.A: Phone confirmations are slower than confirming by email reply
options.B: The calls were made by clerks, not by finance managers
options.C: Phone calls leave no written record of who confirmed each change
options.D: Whoever sent the request controls that number and can confirm

questions.key_concept: A callback works only through a channel the requester does not control: a number already on file, never one given in the request.
questions.pre_read: Ask who chose the phone number that was called, and whether a fraudster could answer it.
questions.correct_explanation: A callback control works because it reaches the real supplier through a channel the requester does not control. A number taken from the change request belongs to whoever sent it, so a fraudster simply answers and confirms the false bank details. Missing call records are a genuine evidence gap, but recording every call to the fraudster's own number would not stop a single fraudulent change.

wrong_explanations.A: Speed is not the weakness; confirming by email reply would be worse, since a hijacked or spoofed mailbox receives the reply.
wrong_explanations.B: Seniority does not fix the channel: a manager calling the number in the request reaches the same fraudster and gets the same false confirmation.
wrong_explanations.C: Call records matter as evidence, but documenting calls to the fraudster's number would still let every fraudulent change through.

tips: Eliminate: A and B, because speed does not make a channel trustworthy, and a senior caller dialing the same number reaches the same fraudster.
Final two: D beats C because better records of a call to the fraudster's number still approve the fraud; the source is not independent.
Exam cue: verify through a channel the attacker cannot control; a number, link or address supplied in the request fails that test.
questions.framework_ref: FinCEN Advisory FIN-2016-A003 (Business Email Compromise)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Business Email Compromise. Callback Design'. Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 5B2.2 (batch Q17: concept practice for a subtopic previously practised only as live-incident FIRST calls or recommendations). Tests why a callback fails when it uses a requester-supplied number; distinct from d5_103, which recommends the callback control. Public sources: FinCEN and ISACA.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds a company's only defense against business email compromise is training finance staff to check sender addresses. What is the MOST likely reason this defense will fail?

options.A: Spam filters remove spoofed messages before staff ever see them
options.B: Fraud often comes from hijacked real mailboxes with correct addresses
options.C: Staff forget most awareness training within a few months of attending
options.D: Attackers can fake the display name shown above the address

questions.key_concept: Business email compromise often uses a hijacked real mailbox, so the sender address checks out; process controls must stop the payment instead.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the thing staff are trained to check would look wrong in every attack.
questions.correct_explanation: Many business email compromise attacks come from a real mailbox the attacker has taken over, at the company or a supplier, so the sender address is exactly right and checking it reveals nothing. That is why callbacks and segregated duties must stop the payment even when the email convinces. Training fading over time is a real limit, but even freshly trained staff cannot spot a correct address.

wrong_explanations.A: Filters catch some spoofed mail but not mail from hijacked real mailboxes, and filtering would not explain why the training fails.
wrong_explanations.C: Refresher training addresses fading knowledge; even freshly trained staff cannot spot fraud sent from a genuine, correctly addressed mailbox.
wrong_explanations.D: Checking the actual address is exactly what exposes a faked display name; a hijacked genuine mailbox is what defeats the check.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because filters miss mail from real mailboxes, and checking the address is what exposes a faked display name.
Final two: B beats C because refresher training cannot help when the fraudulent email comes from a correct, genuine address.
Exam cue: assume someone will be fooled; for payment fraud, prefer process controls such as callbacks over spotting fake emails.
questions.framework_ref: FinCEN Advisory FIN-2016-A003 (Business Email Compromise); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AT-2 (Literacy Training and Awareness)

questions.question: An IS auditor confirms a departing developer's accounts were all disabled on the last day. What is the MOST likely reason a logic bomb the developer planted could still run?

options.A: It fires from inside approved code with the program's own authority
options.B: The developer could still sign in through a shared service account
options.C: Disabled accounts are restored automatically after thirty days
options.D: Antivirus tools cannot scan code held on production servers

questions.key_concept: A logic bomb is hidden code inside approved software that fires on a condition, using the program's authority, so it needs no sign-in.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the hidden code needs its author to sign in before it can run.
questions.correct_explanation: A logic bomb is code hidden inside approved software that fires when a condition is met, such as a date. It runs with the program's own authority, so it needs no account and no sign-in from its author. A shared service account is a real gap to close, but even with it removed the planted code would still fire.

wrong_explanations.B: Shared accounts are a real gap, but a logic bomb needs no sign-in; it would fire even if every account were removed.
wrong_explanations.C: Disabled accounts are not restored automatically, and account status does not matter here, since the code runs without anyone signing in.
wrong_explanations.D: Security tools can scan code held on servers; the issue is that the code sits inside approved software that runs with authority.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because disabled accounts are not restored on their own, and security tools can scan code on servers.
Final two: A beats B because removing every account still leaves the code to fire; it never needed its author to sign in.
Exam cue: a logic bomb hides in approved code, so prevention sits in independent code review before production, not account removal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)

Tests how a logic bomb works (it runs with the program's authority, so account removal cannot stop it); distinct from d5_262, which asks for the preventive control. Public sources: NIST and ISACA.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews environmental risks for a small server room in a leased office building. Which event is MOST LIKELY to occur?

options.A: A brief interruption in the building's utility power supply
options.B: A fire that destroys the server room and its equipment
options.C: Condensation on equipment caused by humidity set too low
options.D: A lightning strike that damages the building's equipment

questions.key_concept: Power disturbances are the most frequent environmental disruption; fire is rarer but far more destructive, so the priority word decides between them.
questions.pre_read: Before weighing options, note whether the stem asks how often an event happens or how much damage it does.
questions.correct_explanation: Brief power interruptions are the most frequent environmental event, which is why uninterruptible power supplies are a baseline control even in small rooms. A destructive fire is the strongest alternative. It would win if the stem asked which event causes the GREATEST impact, but fires are rare, and MOST LIKELY asks how often, not how badly.

wrong_explanations.B: A fire would cause the GREATEST impact, but it is rare; MOST LIKELY asks which event happens most often, and brief power interruptions happen far more often.
wrong_explanations.C: Low humidity causes static discharge, not condensation; condensation comes from humidity that is too high.
wrong_explanations.D: Lightning strikes on a building are rare, and surge protection limits the harm; they happen far less often than brief power interruptions.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because low humidity causes static rather than condensation, and lightning strikes are rare events.
Final two: A beats B because MOST LIKELY asks about frequency; a destructive fire would win only if the stem asked for the GREATEST impact.
Exam cue: MOST LIKELY picks the most frequent event, not the most dramatic; GREATEST picks the most harmful realistic one, which here would be the fire.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-11 (Emergency Power); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.11 (Supporting Utilities)

Original KaiSip item (Oct 2026), written for CISA subtopic 5A2.1 (batch Q18: practice for principles with under ten tagged questions; principle priority-word-decides). The priority word decides: MOST LIKELY picks frequent power disturbances, GREATEST would pick a destructive fire. Closest sibling d5_011 (power protection design); distinct from d5_003 and d5_019 (unmonitored alarms). Public sources: NIST and ISO.

questions.subtopic: Vulnerability Management. Newly Announced Library Flaws
questions.question: A critical flaw is announced in a widely used open-source logging library, and an IS auditor reviews the vulnerability procedure. Which step should the procedure require FIRST?

options.A: Rank affected systems by internet exposure and active exploitation
options.B: Identify every system that runs an affected version
options.C: Run the standard uncredentialed network scan on every host
options.D: Schedule the vendor patch for the next monthly maintenance window

questions.key_concept: Responding to a new library flaw starts with finding every affected system; risk ranking and patching depend on that list.
questions.pre_read: Check whether one plausible step needs the other's result before it can start.
questions.correct_explanation: The procedure must first find every system running an affected version, using software inventories, bills of materials and credentialed scans, because nothing can be ranked or patched until it is found. Ranking by exposure and exploitation is the most tempting alternative. It is the right way to order the work, but it can only rank the systems already identified, so it depends on the inventory step.

wrong_explanations.A: Risk ranking is the right next step, but it can only rank systems already found; a system missed by identification is never ranked.
wrong_explanations.C: An uncredentialed scan sees only what the network exposes, so it usually cannot detect library versions installed inside applications.
wrong_explanations.D: A critical, widely used flaw needs risk-based urgency; waiting for the monthly window leaves exposed systems open longer than needed.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because uncredentialed scans cannot see installed library versions, and the monthly window is too slow for a critical, widely used flaw.
Final two: B beats A because ranking depends on knowing which systems are affected; identification comes first and enables it.
Exam cue: when one plausible option can only work on the other's output, choose the step that produces that output.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-40 Rev 4 (Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning); CIS Controls v8 Control 2 (Inventory and Control of Software Assets); CIS Controls v8 Control 7 (Continuous Vulnerability Management); US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Software Bill of Materials Guidance
